record.paper_title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems
record.context_brief: American football exposure and safety rules
record.original_question: For people who play American football, what amount of playing imposes substantial health risks, including brain-damage concerns such as chronic traumatic encephalopathy and later-life mental-health or cognitive problems, and what rule changes could reduce those risks while preserving the benefits of playing football?

evidence.quote: “The Scars From ‘Bell-Ringing’ Football Tackles” (editorial, 7/29) highlights a high rate of CTE [the type of brain damage football is hypothesized to cause] among former football players who donated their brains for study, and suggests safety concerns about not only pro but also high school football.
However, our research in JAMA Neurology finds among 1950s high school graduates, football players don’t have higher rates of later-life depression or impaired cognition than non-football players.

Many people love playing football and playing promotes physical fitness, teamwork and recreation. More research is needed into what amount of playing imposes substantial risks and what rule changes could reduce risks.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the population of individuals who participate in American (tackle) football. Empirical and clinical evidence indicates that cumulative head impact exposure is associated with chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) — a neurodegenerative tauopathy — and with later-life adverse mental-health and cognitive outcomes such as depression and cognitive impairment, while regular play also confers benefits including physical fitness, teamwork, and recreation.

Develop a quantitative framework that addresses both of the following:

1. (Exposure-risk threshold.) Define a measure E of cumulative football exposure (for example, total years of play, age at first exposure, number of seasons of organized contact play, cumulative count of head impacts, or position-weighted impact severity). Identify the level(s) of E above which the risk of (i) neuropathologically confirmed CTE and (ii) clinically significant later-life depression or cognitive impairment is substantially elevated relative to non-players, in a way that is robust to confounding (selection into football, socioeconomic factors, other sports exposure) and to the cohort effect of changing equipment, rules, and playing styles over time.

2. (Rule-change interventions.) Specify a set of modifiable rule or training interventions (e.g., minimum age for tackling, caps on full-contact practice time per week, restrictions on kickoffs or specific blocking techniques, helmet or mouthguard standards, mandatory exposure monitoring) and quantify the expected reduction in long-term CTE and cognitive-outcome risk under each intervention, while preserving the recreational, fitness, and social benefits of the sport. The framework should make explicit the causal estimands, the assumptions under which they are identifiable from observational or quasi-experimental data, and a strategy (protocol, design, or randomized trial) by which each intervention's effect could be empirically estimated.

Provide either a complete answer to (1) and (2) or a proof that, under stated assumptions, such thresholds and intervention effects cannot be identified from currently available data.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature (2023–2025) provides partial dose–response evidence — e.g., increased CTE odds per year played (~OR 1.30/year), elevated risk for those starting tackle football before age 12, and accelerometer-based associations between cumulative head impacts and CTE pathology — and proposes interventions such as practice-contact caps and age-based tackling restrictions. However, no agreed exposure threshold has been established, donor-brain cohorts suffer from selection bias, and the causal effect of specific rule changes on long-term cognitive outcomes has not been rigorously quantified. The question therefore remains open.

status_evidence.title: Duration of American Football Play and Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy
status_evidence.snippet: Each additional year of American football play increased odds of CTE; a dose-response relationship was observed.
status_evidence.claim: Partial quantitative dose-response evidence exists between years of play and CTE.

status_evidence.title: Leveraging football accelerometer data to quantify associations between repetitive head impacts and CTE
status_evidence.snippet: Cumulative head impacts and linear/rotational accelerations are significantly associated with CTE pathology.
status_evidence.claim: Cumulative impact metrics correlate with CTE, but a clinical threshold is not established.

status_evidence.title: Implementing exposure limits for players in contact team sports
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews principles and practices for setting exposure limits in contact sports; notes lack of agreed thresholds.
status_evidence.claim: Exposure limit policy is still under active development without consensus thresholds.

status_evidence.title: CTE Prevention Protocol
status_evidence.snippet: Recommends contact-practice caps, age cutoffs for tackling, and exposure monitoring as preventive measures.
status_evidence.claim: Proposed rule changes exist but their causal effect on later-life outcomes is not yet quantified.
